analysis.one_liner: Requires mine operators to protect coal miners from COVID-19 with mandatory infection-control plans and reporting.
analysis.headline: The bill drew sponsors from both parties, including the top two senators from coal-producing West Virginia, but never got a hearing or a vote and died in committee at the end of the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ordered the Department of Labor to quickly issue workplace safety rules requiring coal mine operators to write and carry out a plan to stop the spread of COVID-19 underground, supply masks, disinfectant, and other protective gear, and record every work-related COVID-19 infection and death. It also would have required the government to track and investigate COVID-19 cases among miners, including cases where miners already had black lung disease, and report the findings publicly. The bill was introduced by Sen. Joe Manchin and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which took no further action on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal and other miners, who worked in enclosed spaces — shuttles, elevators, break rooms — where the virus spread easily. Miners also tend to be older and many already have reduced lung capacity from dust exposure, putting them at higher risk of severe COVID-19. The bill would have given miners a say in their workplaces' exposure plans and created a public record of infections.

how_it_helps.text: Required mine operators to develop a comprehensive infectious disease exposure control plan with input from miners or their representatives, and to provide personal protective equipment, disinfectant, and medical supplies to limit exposure in mines.
Directed the Department of Labor to issue an emergency temporary standard within 7 days of enactment, in force until a permanent standard replaced it.
Required recording and reporting of all work-related COVID-19 infections and deaths under existing federal mine-safety recordkeeping rules.

Required the government to collect data on COVID-19 among miners, investigate individual cases, look specifically at COVID-19 in miners who also have pneumoconiosis (black lung disease), and publish regular public reports with recommendations.
Ordered the standards to follow CDC and workplace-safety research guidelines, and exempted the emergency rule from several procedural review requirements so it could be issued immediately.

analysis.who_pays: Mine operators, who would have borne the cost of writing exposure control plans, supplying protective equipment and disinfectant, and documenting and reporting infections. Small operators would have faced the same planning and recordkeeping duties as large ones.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have imposed real compliance costs on mine operators, including smaller operations, for planning, protective supplies, and infection recordkeeping.

It would have bypassed several standard rulemaking reviews — the Regulatory Flexibility Act, Paperwork Reduction Act, Unfunded Mandates Reform Act, and the main executive order on regulatory review — to issue the emergency standard within 7 days, trading procedural care for speed.

By the time the bill could realistically have moved, vaccines were widely available and the acute emergency of early 2021 was easing, weakening the case for an emergency standard rather than ordinary guidance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly tens of thousands of coal miners who faced high exposure risk in enclosed underground workplaces — many with already-damaged lungs from dust — the protections were substantial and the direct cost fell on a small number of employers with significant revenue per worker. The main honest objections are the cost to smaller operators and the deliberate bypass of normal regulatory-review procedures, which the emergency framing was designed to justify.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate committee that handles worker safety, which never held a hearing or voted on it, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Joe Manchin introduced the bill on February 2, 2021, with six original cosponsors including both of West Virginia's senators, Manchin (D) and Shelley Moore Capito (R).
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
Six additional senators later signed on as cosponsors — five Democrats and one Republican — for a total of 12 sponsors and cosponsors split across both parties.
The committee took no further action; the bill received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mine operators are better off, because they never had to implement mandatory COVID-19 exposure control plans, supply protective equipment, or record work-related infections and deaths. Miners, who faced elevated risk in enclosed underground workplaces, got no federal protection from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mine operators; no new safety duties

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored and cosponsored by members of both parties — 6 Democrats and 1 Republican among the original sponsors, growing to 5 Democrats and 1 Republican among later cosponsors — so its failure in committee was not a split-roll vote; no vote on it ever occurred.

industries.note: The bill would have required operators to build infection-control plans, buy and provide protective equipment and disinfectant, and document and report every work-related COVID-19 infection and death. Operators benefit from the bill's death because they avoided these costs and avoided a public record of infections in their mines, while miners bear the exposure risk.

The bill would have added rulemaking, surveillance, and investigation duties to the Mine Safety and Health Administration and the Labor Department, funded by appropriations rather than fees on the industry. No new burden falls on them because the bill never passed.
